cases.input: What is an H-1B dependent employer?
cases.notes: H-1B dependent employer definition from I-129 instructions
cases.response:
An H-1B dependent employer is defined in the context as an employer that:

• Has 25 or fewer full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than seven H-1B nonimmigrants;
• Has at least 26 but not more than 50 full-time-equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs more than 12 H-1B nonimmigrants; or
• Has at least 51 full-time equivalent employees who are employed in the United States and employs H-1B nonimmigrants in a number that is equal to at least 15 percent of the number of such full-time-equivalent employees.

cases.input: What is the difference between O-1A and O-1B?
cases.notes: O-1A is sciences/business, O-1B is arts
cases.response:
According to the USCIS guidance, the main difference between O-1A and O-1B is the field of endeavor.

O-1A is for aliens coming to the United States temporarily who have extraordinary ability in the sciences, education, business, or athletics (not including the arts, motion picture, or television industry).

O-1B is for aliens coming to the United States temporarily who have extraordinary ability in the arts or extraordinary achievement in the motion picture or television industry.

Note: This is informational only based on published USCIS guidance, not legal advice.

cases.input: Can an H-1B worker change employers?
cases.notes: H-1B portability / cap-exempt transfer rules
cases.response:
According to the USCIS guidance, yes, an H-1B worker can change employers. However, the process involves filing a new Form I-129 petition with USCIS. 

To change employers, the new employer must file a new Form I-129 petition on behalf of the H-1B worker, and the worker must be in a valid H-1B status. The new petition must include the required documentation, such as a Labor Condition Application (LCA) and proof of the worker's qualifications.

Note: This is informational only based on published USCIS guidance, not legal advice.
